title: A Website vs a Social Page for a Local Business
metaDescription: Plenty of local businesses run on a social profile alone. What that costs, what a one-page site adds, and when you honestly need both.
targetKeyword: do i need a website for my small business
body: A large number of small local businesses have no website. They have a social profile, a phone number, and a listing on a maps app, and they do fine.

So the question is not "is a social page enough" — clearly it can be. The question is what specifically you are giving up, and whether any of it matters for your business. Here is an honest accounting, including what a website does not fix.
What a social profile does better
Genuinely better, not grudgingly:

• Frequency. Posting today's specials takes twelve seconds. No website workflow beats that.
  • Photographs. Your phone, your food, your finished job, posted in the moment.
  • Messaging. People already have the app, and they will message a profile when they would not fill in a form.
  • Distribution. Posts reach people who were not looking for you. A website reaches people who were.
Nothing in this article suggests dropping it.
What it costs you

1. Search. Someone typing "[your trade] near me" gets a maps listing and websites. A social profile is a weak third. The words on a page — your services, your area, your qualifications — are how a search engine understands what you do.
  2. The stuff nobody posts. Prices, hours, service area, insurance, what you do not do. On a profile it is buried in a post from March. On a page it is a section.
  3. Credibility with the cautious. For a purchase involving a key to a house, a child, or four figures, a lot of people still check for a website. Fair or not, its absence reads as smaller.
  4. Control. Your profile's reach, layout and rules belong to a platform. A page does not.
  5. Something to print. A URL on a van or a card should be yours.
What a website does not fix
The part these comparisons usually skip.

A website will not bring you traffic on its own. For a local business the thing that drives enquiries is your maps listing — claimed, complete, with correct hours and real reviews. A site supports that listing; it does not replace it. If you only have time for one, do the listing.

A website will also not post your specials, and it will not have photographs of your work if you build it with Kodely — published sites cannot load an image from any other host and there is no upload path. Your social feed remains your gallery. The site links to it.
What the site actually needs to contain
Less than people think. One page, in this order:

• What you do and where, in the first sentence, using the words people search for.
  • Services with real prices or from-prices.
  • The trust facts: how long, qualifications, insurance, checks.
  • Hours and area covered, as text.
  • One obvious action — a tap-to-call button — repeated top and bottom.
  • Links out to your social profile and your maps listing.

No contact form: a generated site has no server behind it, so a form would silently discard every enquiry. A phone link converts better for local work anyway. The reasoning, and how to build the call to action instead.
The two objections, answered

"It'll take weeks." It takes an afternoon. You describe the business in plain English, a real page is generated, and you refine it by describing changes. Publishing is one click to a kodely.site subdomain.

"I'll never update it." Probably true, and mostly fine — a page listing your services, area and hours goes stale far more slowly than a feed does. When something does change, it is one sentence and a republish, and republishing costs nothing.
Deciding

• Profile only — if you are booked out, your work is entirely visual, and everyone finds you by word of mouth.
  • Add a one-page site — if strangers search for what you do, if people ask the same questions about price and area, or if you want the URL on a van.
  • Either way, do the maps listing. It is free and it does more for a local business than either of them.
